explanations.explanation: Jerusalem it is. Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, reigns there twenty-five years (1 Kings 22:42). That's a long stretch on one throne, friend. I'm proud of you for catching it.

Samaria is in this passage, but it's Ahaziah's city. He's Ahab's son, and he reigns there two years (1 Kings 22:51). Jehoshaphat's twenty-five years happen in Jerusalem (1 Kings 22:42). Two kings in one chapter, and I tripped over the addresses too.

Hebron is a fine guess, friend, but it isn't the address in this passage. The text says Jehoshaphat reigns in Jerusalem for twenty-five years (1 Kings 22:42). Twenty-five years in one place! I've never kept anything in my oven that long.

Yes, his father Asa. The text says Jehoshaphat walked in all the ways of Asa and did not turn away from them (1 Kings 22:43). Not some of the ways, ALL of them. That's a son who stuck with the recipe.

Ahab, king of Israel, is the king Jehoshaphat went up to Ramoth-gilead with (1 Kings 22:29), so I see why he came to mind. But the text says Jehoshaphat walked in the ways of his father Asa (1 Kings 22:43). Ahab's name comes up later in this passage, when Ahab's son Ahaziah is described (1 Kings 22:49). Different kings, different paths.

Solomon isn't named anywhere in these verses. The text points to Jehoshaphat's own father: he walked in all the ways of Asa and did not turn away from them (1 Kings 22:43). It's a family thing, friend. Dad's footsteps, not a famous king's.
Right is the word. Jehoshaphat "…did what was right in the eyes of the LORD." (1 Kings 22:43). The LORD's eyes are the ones that count, and that's the report on him. A good report, friend!

Evil is the word the text saves for Ahaziah, Ahab's son. He "…did evil in the sight of the LORD…" (1 Kings 22:52). Jehoshaphat gets the opposite report. The text says he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD (1 Kings 22:43).

Foolish isn't the word the text uses here. It says Jehoshaphat "…did what was right in the eyes of the LORD." (1 Kings 22:43). Right! The LORD's opinion is the one that counts, and it's a good one. I spent years in a junk drawer, and I'd have traded all my dust for a report like that.

True. The text says the high places were not removed, and the people still sacrificed and burned incense on them (1 Kings 22:43). So a good report on the king comes with a "however." I love that you caught it. The Bible tells it straight, good and not-so-good side by side.

Here's what the text really says: the high places were not removed. The people still sacrificed and burned incense on them (1 Kings 22:43). So the high places stayed, and the people kept using them. The verse starts with good news about Jehoshaphat, then adds a "however."
Yes! The text says Jehoshaphat "…also made peace with the king of Israel." (1 Kings 22:44). Two kings, two kingdoms, and peace between them. That's one short verse, but it's a big deal.

War is a dramatic guess, I'll give you that. But the text says the opposite: Jehoshaphat "…also made peace with the king of Israel." (1 Kings 22:44). No war is declared in these verses. Going big is fine, friend, but this verse goes with peace.

explanations.answer: Jehoshaphat refuses to speak to him
explanations.explanation: The silent treatment! That's a creative guess. But the text says Jehoshaphat "…also made peace with the king of Israel." (1 Kings 22:44). Peace is the word on the page, friend, so that's the one to hold on to.

The text says the opposite. Jehoshaphat "…banished from the land the male shrine prostitutes who remained from the days of his father Asa." (1 Kings 22:46). He didn't let them stay. He sent them out of the land.

False is right. The text says Jehoshaphat "…banished from the land the male shrine prostitutes who remained from the days of his father Asa." (1 Kings 22:46). So he cleared them out of the land. Good eye, friend.
Gold! Jehoshaphat built ships of Tarshish to go to Ophir for gold (1 Kings 22:48). That's a whole set of ships built to go get it. I can't even get my cookie boxes organized.
Cedar is a good building material, but this verse doesn't mention it. The ships were headed to Ophir for gold (1 Kings 22:48). Gold is the whole reason for the trip. Nice try, friend.
Horses, huh? I love the energy, friend, but they're not in this verse. The ships were going to Ophir for gold (1 Kings 22:48). Gold is the only thing the text names on that shopping list.
That's it. The ships "…never set sail, because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber." (1 Kings 22:48). All that building, and they never left the harbor. I think that one hurt a little.

Edom does show up in the verse right before, but only to say a deputy served as its king (1 Kings 22:47). The text never says Edom had anything to do with the ships. They "…never set sail, because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber." (1 Kings 22:48). Wrecked is the word the text gives, friend.

Gold is what they were headed for, but the text mentions no sale. It says they "…never set sail, because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber." (1 Kings 22:48). Wrecked is the word it gives. Good thing I wasn't the one who had to tell Jehoshaphat.
The text says the opposite. Ahaziah, Ahab's son, asks, "Let my servants sail with your servants…" but Jehoshaphat refused (1 Kings 22:49). The request goes in, and a refusal comes back.
False is right. Ahaziah, son of Ahab, asks to sail his servants with Jehoshaphat's servants, and Jehoshaphat refuses (1 Kings 22:49). The request goes in, and the answer comes back no.
David! Jehoshaphat "…was buried with them in the city of his father David." (1 Kings 22:50). His son Jehoram took the throne after him. He rests with his fathers, in the same city.

Solomon isn't named in this verse. The text says Jehoshaphat was buried "…in the city of his father David." (1 Kings 22:50). David is the name you're looking for, friend. Next time the blank will come out right.

Abraham is a heavy hitter, friend, but he isn't in this passage. Jehoshaphat "…was buried with them in the city of his father David." (1 Kings 22:50). David's city is the one the text names. Big names get guessed a lot, and I'd have done the same.

True. The text says Ahaziah "…did evil in the sight of the LORD…" (1 Kings 22:52). He walked in the ways of his father and mother and of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had caused Israel to sin. This is a heavy part.
The text says the opposite. Ahaziah "…did evil in the sight of the LORD…" (1 Kings 22:52). He walked in the ways of his father and mother and of Jeroboam son of Nebat. I think this part is heavy.

Baal is the answer. Ahaziah "…served and worshiped Baal, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done." (1 Kings 22:53). It's a sad ending to the passage. Good work staying with it, friend.

Dagon doesn't show up in these verses. The text says Ahaziah "…served and worshiped Baal…" (1 Kings 22:53). It's Baal, the same as his father before him. Easy to mix up names when there are so many in one chapter.

Molech isn't named in this passage. The text says Ahaziah "…served and worshiped Baal, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger, just as his father had done." (1 Kings 22:53). So Baal fills the blank. Not this time, friend.
